authority_boundary: This source-grounded profile supports a provisional Library note. It does not verify present facts, produce a historical base rate, authorize publication, or supply action authority.
central_question_or_situation: What becomes visible when history is read as the relation between innumerable situated acts rather than as the execution of a sovereign will?
failure_modes: Turning Tolstoy's critique of command into a denial that institutions or leaders matter.
Treating the novel's philosophy of history as an empirically established social law.
Using an unidentified English translation as if it settled Russian wording.

affective_movements: Humility before the scale of collective action and the opacity of historical causation.
forms_of_attention: Look beneath a command for the chain of executable relations that made it effective.
Distinguish retrospective narrative compression from causal explanation.
mechanisms: Commands become effective only when they coincide with a corresponding series of events and executors.
Historical narration compresses many contingent acts into the will of a visible leader.
perceptual_patterns: Ask which orders failed, which were executable, and which agents carried an event into being.
propositions: Power is a relation between expressed will and execution, not a self-sufficient cause.
The apparent freedom or necessity of action changes with temporal, causal, and relational distance.
symbolic_structures: The retrospective label of the great man

common_misreadings: Reducing distributed causation to leaderlessness or fatalism.
internal_tensions: The work denies sovereign command as sufficient cause while retaining power as an observable relation.
rival_readings: A novelistic correction to command-centered historiography

anti_analogy: Do not infer that visible leaders are causally irrelevant in every modern institution.
Do not convert literary-historical argument into a quantitative base rate.

scope_conditions: The note uses the admitted Project Gutenberg English body of War and Peace; its translator is unresolved in registry metadata.
No Russian original-language body is claimed or silently substituted.
The profile remains note-first and creates no operational route.
synopsis: War and Peace joins narrative scale to an explicit critique of command-centered history. Its closing argument treats power as a relation between orders and execution, emphasizes the selection of executable commands from innumerable failures, and resists explaining collective movement through the will of a few named actors.

passage_anchors.anchor_summary: Rejects command as an immediate cause when orders are often ineffective and defines power as the relation between will and execution.
Makes command effective only through a corresponding series of events and locates commanders at the smallest point of direct participation.
Describes freedom and necessity as reciprocal perceptions conditioned by relation, time, and causal knowledge.

uncertainties: The registry does not identify the English translator of the admitted body.
The note does not establish equivalence with Tolstoy's Russian text.
The relation between the epilogue's explicit theory and the novel's enacted plurality remains interpretive.
